reason: The typological expectation is strong enough that declining it has to be written down. Ether 14 opens with 'a great curse upon the land, because of the iniquity of the people' and proceeds to siege, burned cities, unburied dead and national extinction, which is the programme of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 in order. Deuteronomy 28:29-31 is the closest the KJV comes to the specific form the curse takes here — 'thou shalt be only oppressed and spoiled evermore, and no man shall save thee … thine ox shall be slain before thine eyes, and thou shalt not eat thereof … and thou shalt have none to rescue them' — property removed from a man's hands with no redress. But there is not one shared distinctive word, and the Book of Mormon's curse is not the Deuteronomic list: it is a specific and non-biblical thing, the disappearance of tools and swords laid down, which the record has already used at Helaman 13:31-36 ('their treasures … become slippery') and will use again at Mormon 1:18. Deuteronomy's curses take away crops, health, children and freedom; none of them makes objects vanish off a shelf. The land-curse frame is the Book of Mormon's own, established at Ether 2:8-11 for this land specifically, and it does not need Deuteronomy to explain it. Recorded so that a reader who reaches for Leviticus 26 or Deuteronomy 28 here is told the catalogue reached for them too and could not make the wording bear it.

The highest-scoring candidate on the opening verse and it is connective tissue. 'Because of the iniquity of the people' is one of the Book of Mormon's commonest editorial formulas, and 'the iniquity of the' is a KJV genitive chain that carries no source with it. Lamentations 4:6 is about Sodom's overthrow being quicker and kinder than Jerusalem's siege; nothing else in it touches Ether 14. Covered by the standing exclusion on connective matches (CONVENTIONS §5) and listed only because it ranked first here.

A genuine KJV singleton in an opposed sense, and the kind of match a careful reader will find and wonder about. “did cleave unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day' — the survivors of Baal-peor, defined by what they held onto. Ether 14:2 reads 'every man did cleave unto that which was his own, with his hands', and every man in it dies. The inversion is neat enough to be tempting and that is exactly why it is not evidence: 'cleave unto' is ordinary KJV register (thirteen verses), the past-tense auxiliary 'did' is the Book of Mormon's default narrative form on nearly every verb in this chapter ('did cleave', 'did march', 'did smite', 'did pursue', 'did burn'), and the three-word string is therefore produced by the text's own grammar rather than by Deuteronomy. Where the KJV's verb takes God as its object and means covenant fidelity, the Book of Mormon's takes movable property and means a man's fists closed on it.

Rarity 1.50 and a five-word run, and it is a prepositional accident. Psalm 89:25 is the Davidic covenant — 'I will set his hand also in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers' — where the right hand is imperial reach. Ether 14:2's right hand is holding a sword hilt. The run exists because both sentences happen to put a body part in a place. No other contact.

Worth an entry because the borrowing-and-lending pair is Deuteronomic and the chapter is a curse chapter, so the pull is real. Deuteronomy 28:12 and 15:6 make lending-without-borrowing the sign of blessing, and 28:44 makes the reverse the sign of curse; if Ether 14:2 were following that frame it would say the Jaredites were reduced to borrowing. It says the opposite of both: nobody lends and nobody borrows, because credit itself has become impossible. That is a third state Deuteronomy never describes, and the verbal contact is two ordinary words that the KJV uses of Israelite neighbours (Exodus 22:14) and Egyptian jewels (Exodus 3:22, 11:2) as readily as of covenant blessing. The clause is doing the Book of Mormon's own work — showing what the slippery-treasures curse does to exchange — and does not need Deuteronomy 28 to be read.

sharedText: for the space of two years
reason: Dating boilerplate, and this entry covers the same candidate wherever it recurs in the chapter — 14:7 ('for the space of two years', Acts 19:10 again) and 14:26 ('for the space of three days', Acts 19:8). 'For the space of' is the King James Bible's standard way of measuring a duration and the Book of Mormon's too; Acts 19 ranks only because Paul's Ephesian residence happened to last two years. A Jaredite pretender's exile in the wilderness of Akish and a two-year preaching in the school of Tyrannus have nothing else in common. No further 'space of' candidates in this chapter are listed individually.

Top candidate on the verse and pure syntax. Luke 22:56 is the servant girl noticing Peter by the fire; Ether 14:9 is a high priest murdering a king on his throne. The four-word run is the English for observing somebody in a seated posture. Recorded because the verse is a striking one — regicide on the throne, in one sentence — and a reader may expect the catalogue to have found something for it. There is a real biblical type here (Ehud and Eglon at Judges 3:20, Ish-bosheth at 2 Samuel 4:5-7, Sennacherib at 2 Kings 19:37) but Ether 14:9 gives it eighteen words and no distinctive vocabulary at all; nothing in the KJV can be shown to stand behind them.

The joint highest-scoring candidate in the chapter at rarity 2.00, and worthless. 'The face of the land' and 'the face of the earth' are among the Book of Mormon's most frequent phrases, and 'the whole face of the' is that phrase plus a quantifier; the chapter uses it four times in six verses (14:19, 14:21, 14:22, 14:23). Genesis 2:6 is the mist that watered the ground before it rained. Covered by the standing exclusion on connective matches; listed once here because of its rank, and this entry covers 'upon all the face of' at 14:23 (ranked to Ezekiel 34:6) as well.

“shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22 — 'without shedding of blood is no remission' — and Ether 14:22 uses the phrase twice in a single clause, 'from the shedding of blood, to the shedding of blood', which looks like the strongest kind of evidence until it is counted against the Book of Mormon itself. The phrase occurs in thirteen Book of Mormon verses, most of them the Nephite war chapters (Alma 26:24, 48:14, 48:16, 48:23, 52:4, 58:28) where it means exactly what it means here, warfare, and where it is already fixed vocabulary long before Ether. Whatever Hebrews 9:22 contributed to the Book of Mormon's idiom, it contributed elsewhere; a reader wanting the atonement sense should look at Alma 34:13, which is the verse that argues about remission of sins. Ether 14:22's doubling is a rhetorical figure on a house phrase, not a quotation.

The most seductive candidate in the chapter and it has to be declined at length. “the scent thereof” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 14:7, and Ether 14:23 uses it twice — a KJV singleton reproduced twice in a single verse is normally decisive. Three things defeat it. First, the sense is not merely different but perfectly opposed: Hosea 14:7's scent is the fragrance of restored Israel, 'as the wine of Lebanon', in the chapter where the nation is healed after the sword; Ether 14:23's is the stench of unburied corpses that keeps a whole land awake. Second, the Book of Mormon has its own precedent for the phrase in precisely this sense — Alma 16:11, the corpses of Ammonihah, 'so great was the scent thereof, that the people did not go in to possess the land … for many years' — which is the same word, the same referent, and the same consequence of a land made uninhabitable by its own dead. Ether 14:23 is following Alma 16:11, not Hosea. Third, 'thereof' is not evidence of anything: it is an 1830 tic used three more times in this chapter alone ('the hilt of his sword thereof' 14:2, 'the cities thereof' 14:17, 'in the stead thereof' 14:16), and the 1920 edition deleted two of those three as redundant, which is the editors' own testimony that they read it as a verbal habit rather than as borrowed language. 'Scent' plus the Book of Mormon's default possessive produces this string without any help from Hosea.

This is the chapter's best-looking machine candidate and the register is the right place for it. “the fulness of his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 20:22 ('in the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits'), and the very next verse supplies the missing noun: “fury of his wrath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 20:23. So Ether 14:25's 'the Lord did visit them in the fulness of his wrath' can be read as a fusion of two consecutive KJV singletons, in a Joban speech about the portion of the wicked man whose prosperity turns to destruction — a very attractive reading, and wrong. 'The fulness of his wrath' is a Book of Mormon formula with a history: 1 Nephi 22:17, 2 Nephi 1:17, and — decisively — Ether 2:8 and 2:9, twelve chapters earlier in this same book, where it is the technical term for what comes on any nation that possesses this land and will not serve God ('they shall be swept off when the fulness of his wrath shall come upon them … when they are ripened in iniquity'). Ether 14:25 is the fulfilment notice for Ether 2:9 and quotes it, not Job. Note the incidental finding: the KJV never says 'fulness of his wrath' at all — it says 'fierceness of his wrath' — so the Book of Mormon's phrase is its own coinage, and where that coinage came from is a question for 1 Nephi 22:17, not for this verse.

“sound a trumpet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the Sermon on the Mount forbidding it: 'when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do.' Ether 14:28's trumpet is a battlefield challenge sounded from a hill to invite an opposing army down. Nothing but the collocation is shared, and the collocation is the only way English says the thing. The KJV's own war-trumpets are blown, not sounded (Numbers 10:9, Judges 6:34), which is what makes Matthew 6:2 the singleton; the Book of Mormon's verb choice is not a borrowing but a nineteenth-century idiom the translation uses freely.

sharedText: (two armies, facing high ground, a valley between)
reason: A cross-reference as much as an exclusion. The staging of 14:28-29 is 1 Samuel 17:1-3 exactly — one army in the valley of Corihor, the other encamped in the valley of Shurr by the hill Comnor, the challenger gathering his forces on the height and calling the other side out to fight — and it comes eighteen verses after a man of great stature (14:10) and ten after the cry 'Who can stand before the army of Shiz?' (14:18). The Goliath frame is real and is argued in this catalogue, but it is argued where the wording is: see the links at 14:10 (2 Samuel 21:20 and 1 Samuel 10:23) and 14:18 (Deuteronomy 9:2). Verse 28 itself shares not one distinctive word with 1 Samuel 17 — the Book of Mormon's armies pitch tents in valleys and gather on hills throughout Alma without any help from the Philistines — so no link is filed here. A reader who sees David and Goliath in this chapter is seeing something the catalogue also sees, two verses earlier.

sharedText: the second time ... the third time
reason: Rarity 1.39 on a triple repetition, and the KJV verse behind it is Elijah on Carmel telling his servants to drench the altar: 'Do it the second time … Do it the third time.' Ether 14:29's threefold repetition is three failed assaults on a hill. Both texts use the KJV's ordinal formula for a thing done three times, which is the whole of the resemblance; the formula is not distinctive enough to carry a source, and the Book of Mormon uses it independently whenever it counts anything (compare the second and third watches, the second and third times messengers are sent). Nothing of Carmel — no altar, no water, no fire, no contest of gods — is present.

sharedText: (the wounded king carried out of the battle)
reason: The type-scene pulls and the wording will not bear it, so it goes in the register rather than the catalogue. Coriantumr takes many deep wounds, loses his blood, faints and is 'carried away as though he were dead'; Ahab is smitten between the joints of the harness, tells his driver 'carry me out of the host; for I am wounded', is stayed up in his chariot, and 'the blood ran out of the wound' until he dies at even (1 Kings 22:34-35). Four elements in common and not one shared phrase — “as though he were dead” occurs in no KJV verse, and neither does “deep wounds”. The decisive objection is the outcome. The Ahab scene exists to kill the king the prophet condemned; Ether 14:30 exists to not kill him, because 14:24 has just cited the oracle that Coriantumr should not fall by the sword, and his survival of an apparently mortal wounding is the oracle working. Acts 14:19, where Paul is stoned and dragged out 'supposing he had been dead' and then gets up, is the closer analogue for the survival, and it is no closer verbally. The catalogue declines both.
